newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Britain faces court action for breaking EU rules.
newsitem.headline: Britain faces court action for breaking EU rules.

text.p: The European Commission said on Friday it had decided to take Britain before the European Court for breaking European Union rules on public procurement.

The EU executive said it would also send reasoned opinions -- the final legal step before court action -- to Britain, Germany, Belgium and Portugal for violating the public procurement rules which require that public contracts be put up for competitive tender.
If it does not get a satisfactory reply within two months, the Commission may refer these matters to the Luxembourg court.
The Commission said firms which had suffered loss as a result of decisions to award contracts had lodged complaints.

"These specific cases show that the practical application of public procurement legislation still poses a number of problems," EU Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti said in a Commission statement.
He said public procurement was worth 11.5 percent of EU gross domestic product and was one of the main targets of a plan to improve the functioning of the EU's single market.
"In the meantime I will be sure to follow up infringement proceedings against any member state which fails to apply the public procurement directive," he said.

The Commission said its decision to refer Britain to the court over the way the Audit Commission's appointed external auditors to all local authorities in England and Wales for 1992 and 1993 would not be executed before early February to allow final discssions to solve the problem.

The Commission also decided to send three reasoned opinions to Britain, among other things for failure to ensure that the post office fulfilled its obligations under the EU's public supplies directive.

It accused Germany of incorrect application of the EU's services directive and Belgium of infringing rules on public works contracts. Portugal has been sent four such reasoned opinions for different cases of breaking the public procurement rules.
